Running a file X86.Exe.writeChecked accepted, with arguments s1 ... sk, behaves as follows. The kernel loads it as its program headers say: the file read and execute at 0x400000, a zero-filled read-write segment at 0x10000000 holding the program stack at its bottom and the region above it, nothing executable on the stack, and enters the shell with the System V x86-64 initial stack (argc, argv). So a run makes exactly prctl, seccomp, write (once unless the kernel writes part of the line) and exit. specification_assumptions.assumption: The shell's code is not assumed: X86.Exe.Process.shell_sound proves, for every file X86.Exe.Machine.writeChecked accepts, that the generic shell realises the session model (X0-P). What is assumed is the platform the theorem takes as hypotheses, exactly three specification modules, one platform fact, and the environment they describe. (1) Process.Loaded (IxCC/X86/Exe/Process/Loaded.lean): the kernel's ELF loader and initial stack (System V gABI, Program Loading; x86-64 psABI, Initial Stack and Register State): rip is the entry the checked header gives (the shell's first byte), the file's bytes are at 0x400000, and rsp points at argc, argv[0] to argv[argc - 1] and a null pointer, argv[i] for i >= 1 pointing at the bytes of the i-th argument and a NUL, every word and byte of the block outside the frame's zero-filled segments; nothing is assumed of permissions, the zero fill, other registers or the flags. (2) Process.Syscall (IxCC/X86/Exe/Process/Syscall.lean): the syscall(2) convention (the number in rax, the arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9, the result in rax, rcx and r11 written by the instruction, every other register and the memory unchanged on return), prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, ...) and seccomp(SECCOMP_SET_MODE_FILTER, 0, prog) returning any result, write(fd, buf, count) recording the count bytes at buf and returning a byte count no larger than count when non-negative (else -errno), and exit (system call 60) ending the process; any other call, or prctl and seccomp with other arguments, may do anything. (3) Process.Step (IxCC/X86/Exe/Process/Step.lean): the processor is the byte machine (x86-v0-local-semantics) fetching from the file, which the loader maps read-and-execute (so a store of the process there faults), with the system call where the byte decoder decodes nothing and the bytes are 0F 05; where the byte machine does not say what the processor does, nothing is promised: where the decoder decodes nothing and the bytes are not 0F 05 (which includes every rip outside the file) and where the byte machine stops on a condition over a flag it leaves undefined, the process may step to any state with any system call or none, or end. None of these is a fault of the processor: undecoded bytes are in general instructions it runs, a branch on an undefined flag goes one way, and outside the file it runs whatever is mapped there. (4) A memory fault or a divide error ends the process with no further system call: the processor raises an exception, the kernel sends SIGSEGV, SIGBUS or SIGFPE, and its default action applies, no handler being installed (execve resets handlers; the kernel forces the default action of a fault's signal that is ignored or blocked; the shell installs none, its only system calls before a call the model shows stuck being prctl, seccomp, write and exit, which shell_sound proves). (5) The environment: the specifications describe the kernel's own behaviour for a process nothing outside it interferes with. (a) No tracer is attached: a ptrace tracer can change system-call results, registers and memory and suppress a fault's signal (strace -e inject=exit:error=EPERM makes exit return, and the shell's exit block, which jumps back to itself, then repeats the call, a trace no theorem allows). (b) No seccomp filter or supervisor installed by an ancestor changes what write, exit, prctl or seccomp do or return: a filter answering exit with an error makes it return as in (a), and a user-notification supervisor answering write with more than its count makes the report loop step past its message and write bytes no theorem allows (a filter that kills the process does no harm). (c) No other process writes the process's memory or the file it is mapped from: such a writer changes the bytes the shell writes or the instructions the processor runs. (d) The process has one thread: execve leaves one and the shell creates none; with another, memory could change between instructions, and system call 60, which ends only the calling thread, would not end the process. Nothing else is assumed by this entry: the theorems allow a memory fault at any access, after which the trace ends, say nothing of progress, and claim nothing past the point where the source step goes wrong; a state where Process.Step promises nothing is reached only past that point (machine_exe_unspecified).
